full_title: OFFICE OF THE COURT ADMINISTRATOR, COMPLAINANT, VS. WINLOVE M. DUMAYAS, FORMER PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 59, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, MAKATI CITY, RESPONDENT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Gross ignorance of the law vs. mere error of judgment
Retroactive application of the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability to pending cases
Jurisdiction over a judge separated from service while the case is pending (Section 23, CJCA)
Flip-flopping rulings; correction of an error on motion for reconsideration
Judgment on compromise; criminal liability cannot be compromised (Civil Code, Art. 2034)

other_subjects.subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Obligations and Contracts > B. Contracts > 5. Interpretation of Contracts

doctrine:
**A judge is not administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law for an erroneous order issued in a judicial capacity, absent proof of bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or similar motive.** Gross ignorance of the law is the disregard of basic rules and settled jurisprudence. Where the law is straightforward and the facts evident, failing to know it or acting as if one does not know it is gross ignorance, without need to prove malice. Otherwise, the order must not only be erroneous; it must be shown that the judge was moved by bad faith, dishonesty, hatred, or some like motive (reiterating Cayabyab v. Judge Pangilinan, Jr.). Misreading a contractual provision that is not explicit, or issuing a wrong order that the judge later corrects on a motion for reconsideration, is an error of judgment, not gross ignorance. Reversing oneself, by itself, is not an infraction, and ill motive cannot be presumed.

**The 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA, A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC, effective December 21, 2025) applies to all pending and future cases** under its transitory clause (General Provisions, Section 1), unless the Court finds that retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. **Under Section 23 of the CJCA, a judge's separation from the service after the administrative case was instituted does not deprive the Court of jurisdiction.** If the judge is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal, the Court may impose, in lieu of dismissal, forfeiture of all or part of the benefits (never accrued leave credits) and disqualification from public office, and/or a fine.

Settled rules restated in the analysis: once a compromise agreement is approved by a final order, it becomes a judgment that the court has the ministerial duty to enforce and cannot modify; and under Article 2034 of the Civil Code, criminal liability cannot be the subject of a compromise.
facts:
In a Decision dated September 13, 2017 in Team Image Entertainment, Inc. v. Solar Team Entertainment, Inc. (G.R. Nos. 191652 and 191658), the Court referred to the OCA, as a regular administrative matter, the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order issued by Judge Winlove M. Dumayas of RTC Makati, Branch 59, in Civil Case No. 00-1122. It directed him to explain (1) why he ordered a PHP 2 million deposit with the Office of the Clerk of Court (OCC) and (2) why he reversed himself several times on whether Team Image could suspend payments and whether criminal cases could be dismissed under the parties' compromise agreement.

Solar Team and Team Image executed a Compromise Agreement on April 28, 2003, which Judge Dumayas approved on April 30, 2003. Item No. 24 provided that if a party breached the agreement, the aggrieved party was entitled to an immediate writ of execution and "the guilty party shall pay the innocent party" PHP 2 million as liquidated damages. It also said the innocent party could invoke the principle of reciprocity of obligations. Judge Dumayas then issued a string of conflicting orders. He allowed Team Image to suspend payments (April 29, 2004) and later set this aside (November 23, 2004). He granted a writ to enforce PHP 2 million in liquidated damages against Solar Team and again allowed suspension (November 3, 2005). On January 21, 2008, he allowed suspension, ordered Solar Team's William Tieng to cause the dismissal of criminal cases against Team Image's president, and imposed other liabilities.

In the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order, Judge Dumayas set aside all his earlier orders allowing suspension of payments and declared Team Image in default. He also set aside the January 21, 2008 order, including the directive to dismiss the criminal cases. Without deciding whether Solar Team had actually breached the agreement, he granted Solar Team's motion to deposit the PHP 2 million with the OCC, to be released only after the parties' obligations and Solar Team's alleged breach were finally resolved. The CA reversed the deposit order, and the Supreme Court in 2017 also set it aside, applying legal compensation between the parties' equal PHP 2 million liabilities.

In his Comment, Judge Dumayas said he acted in the proper exercise of his judicial functions and his appreciation of the evidence, with no bad faith or corrupt motive. Meanwhile, in a separate case (A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435, Decision of March 6, 2018), he had been dismissed from the service for gross ignorance of the law or procedure and gross misconduct. The JIB (Report of November 15, 2023) recommended a finding of gross ignorance of the law for the deposit order and a PHP 200,000 fine. It recommended no liability for the flip-flopping, because his final rulings on those two points were upheld.
issues: Whether the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability applies to this case, which was pending when the Code took effect.
Whether respondent's dismissal from the service in another case deprived the Court of jurisdiction over this administrative case.

Whether respondent is guilty of gross ignorance of the law for issuing the May 19, 2008 Omnibus Order allowing Solar Team to deposit the PHP 2 million liquidated damages with the OCC instead of paying it to Team Image.

Whether respondent is administratively liable for repeatedly reversing himself on whether Team Image could suspend payments and whether the criminal cases could be dismissed under the compromise agreement.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the 2025 CJCA applies.** The CJCA, approved on November 11, 2025 and effective December 21, 2025, applies to all pending and future cases under its transitory clause, except where retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. The Court found no compelling reason why applying it to respondent would be unfeasible or unjust.

**2. No, the Court retained jurisdiction.** Under Section 23 of the CJCA, if a respondent is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal that can no longer be imposed because of a prior separation from the service (except death), the Court may impose forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification, and/or a fine. This case was instituted on September 13, 2017, when the Court promulgated its Decision in G.R. Nos. 191652 and 191658. Respondent was dismissed in A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435 only on March 6, 2018. **His supervening separation during the pendency of the case does not prevent the Court from imposing sanctions if he is found liable.**

**3. No gross ignorance for the deposit order.** The Court restated the rule that a compromise agreement approved by final order becomes an enforceable judgment that the court cannot modify. It also noted that Item No. 24 required the guilty party to *pay* the innocent party and did not mention deposit in court. Still, there was "no indication or proof" that the order was attended by bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, or corruption. Nor was the Court convinced that respondent was unaware of the compromise terms or of the rule. He had earlier, on November 3, 2005, issued a writ to enforce direct payment of the PHP 2 million. In the May 19, 2008 Order he expressly tied the deposit to the unresolved question of whether Solar Team had breached the agreement. His "need to justify" the deposit "belies any suspicion of ignorance of the basic principles of law and the terms of the Compromise Agreement." **In the absence of fraud, dishonesty, or corruption, the order, done in his judicial capacity, is not subject to disciplinary action.**

**4. No liability for the reversals.** (a) *Suspension of payments.* Whether suspension was allowed required interpreting Item No. 24. Its first sentence speaks of a writ of execution, but its second gives the innocent party the right to invoke reciprocity of obligations. The CA read the agreement as allowing suspension. Under Article 1370 of the Civil Code, clear terms control, but Item No. 24 "is not explicit" on suspension, so the provision is not "so elementary" that misreading it makes a judge liable. An erroneous interpretation is an error of judgment. Reversing himself several times "does not warrant a finding that respondent committed an infraction," and the Court cannot speculate on ill motive without evidence. (b) *Dismissal of criminal cases.* Criminal liability cannot be compromised (Art. 2034, Civil Code), so the January 21, 2008 directive to cause the dismissal of the criminal cases was wrong. But **a motion for reconsideration exists precisely to let the court correct its errors, and respondent "rightly" reversed the order on Solar Team's motion. The earlier order was therefore a mere error of judgment, not gross ignorance.**

The Court added that respondent should have been more circumspect to avoid "flipflopping rulings," and that judges should avoid even the appearance of indecisiveness. Because he had already been dismissed from the service, however, a reminder or warning "no longer has practical value."
disposition: The administrative case against former Presiding Judge Winlove M. Dumayas, Branch 59, RTC, Makati City, was DISMISSED. The Court did not adopt the JIB's recommendation of a PHP 200,000 fine for gross ignorance of the law.

bar_questions.q: In a collection suit, Judge Reyes approved a compromise agreement providing that a party who breaches it "shall pay the innocent party" PHP 1 million as liquidated damages, enforceable by writ of execution. Years later, Debtor Corp. moved for execution, claiming Creditor Inc. had breached the agreement. Judge Reyes had earlier issued a writ for the direct payment of the PHP 1 million. In a later order, however, he allowed Creditor Inc. to deposit the PHP 1 million with the Office of the Clerk of Court instead, explaining that it would be released only after the question of Creditor Inc.'s breach was finally resolved. The Court of Appeals set aside the deposit order as contrary to the compromise judgment. Debtor Corp. then charged Judge Reyes with gross ignorance of the law. Nothing in the record shows bad faith, fraud, or corruption. Should Judge Reyes be held liable?

alac.answer: No. Judge Reyes is not liable for gross ignorance of the law. The deposit order, though erroneous, was an error of judgment made in his judicial capacity.
alac.legal_basis: Gross ignorance of the law is the disregard of basic rules and settled jurisprudence. Unless the law violated is so elementary that disregarding it shows ignorance in itself, a judge is liable only if the erroneous order was moved by bad faith, fraud, dishonesty, corruption, or a similar motive. In the absence of these, acts of a judge in his judicial capacity are not subject to disciplinary action even if erroneous. In OCA v. Judge Dumayas (A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026), the Court applied this rule to a judge who allowed a deposit of liquidated damages with the clerk of court instead of payment to the innocent party under a compromise judgment.
alac.application: A compromise judgment must be enforced as written, so the deposit order was wrong, as the CA held. But nothing shows bad faith, fraud, or corruption. Judge Reyes was plainly aware of the compromise terms and of the rule on compromise judgments: he had earlier ordered direct payment. He also explained why he required a deposit instead, pending resolution of Creditor Inc.'s alleged breach. As in Dumayas, the need to justify the departure belies ignorance of basic law. Debtor Corp.'s remedy against the error was judicial, and it already obtained relief from the CA.
alac.conclusion: The administrative complaint for gross ignorance of the law should be dismissed.

bar_questions.q: A compromise agreement approved by Judge Lim in a civil case required each party to "cause the dismissal of all civil and criminal cases" filed against the other. On Mario's motion, Judge Lim ordered Nestor to cause the dismissal of an estafa case pending against Mario in another court. Nestor moved for reconsideration, and Judge Lim set aside that order, ruling that criminal liability cannot be compromised. Earlier, on the separate question of whether the compromise allowed a party to suspend payments, Judge Lim had also reversed himself twice. The provision on remedies was not explicit on this point. Mario charged Judge Lim with gross ignorance of the law and with "flip-flopping." Will the complaint prosper?

alac.answer: No. Both the corrected order on the estafa case and the reversals on suspension of payments are errors of judgment, not gross ignorance of the law.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 2034 of the Civil Code, a compromise may cover the civil liability arising from an offense but does not extinguish the public action for the penalty; criminal liability cannot be compromised. A motion for reconsideration exists to give the court a chance to correct its errors. A judge who corrects an erroneous order on reconsideration commits a mere error of judgment. Reversing oneself, by itself, is not an infraction, and misreading a contractual provision that is not explicit (Art. 1370, Civil Code) is not gross ignorance. (OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026)
alac.application: Judge Lim's first order directing Nestor to cause the dismissal of the estafa case was wrong, because criminal liability cannot be compromised. But he corrected it on Nestor's motion for reconsideration, which is exactly what that motion is for. On suspension of payments, the compromise was not explicit, so his changing readings were errors of interpretation. No evidence shows bad faith or ill motive, and the Court will not presume it from the reversals alone. At most, Judge Lim may be reminded to be more circumspect to avoid indecisive rulings.
alac.conclusion: The complaint will not prosper because Judge Lim committed only errors of judgment, which are not administratively punishable absent bad faith.

bar_questions.q: In March 2024, the Supreme Court referred to the OCA, for docketing as an administrative matter, an order issued by Judge Santos. In 2025, while that matter was pending, Judge Santos was dismissed from the service in a different administrative case. In 2026 the Court is ready to decide the first matter. (a) Has the Court lost jurisdiction because Judge Santos is no longer in the service? (b) Which rules govern, and if Judge Santos is found guilty of an offense that merits dismissal, what penalties may still be imposed?

alac.answer: (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction. (b) The 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability governs. In lieu of dismissal, the Court may impose forfeiture of all or part of his benefits (except accrued leave credits) and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, and/or a fine.
alac.legal_basis: Under its transitory clause, the 2025 CJCA (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC, effective December 21, 2025) applies to all pending and future cases, unless the Court finds that retroactive application would not be feasible or would work injustice. Under Section 23 of the CJCA, if a respondent is found liable for an offense meriting dismissal but dismissal can no longer be imposed because of prior resignation, retirement, or other separation (except death), the Court may impose (a) forfeiture of all or part of the benefits, never including accrued leave credits, and disqualification from reinstatement or appointment to any public office, including GOCCs; and/or (b) a fine. A separation that occurs after the administrative case was instituted does not divest the Court of jurisdiction. (OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-19-2570, January 28, 2026)
alac.application: The case against Judge Santos was instituted in March 2024, while he was still in the service. His dismissal in 2025 in another case came after the Court's jurisdiction had attached. Since the case was still pending when the CJCA took effect, the CJCA applies, and nothing suggests that applying it would be unfeasible or unjust. Dismissal can no longer be imposed on a judge already dismissed, but the Court may order forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits), disqualification from public office, and/or a fine.
alac.conclusion: The Court keeps jurisdiction and, under the 2025 CJCA, may impose forfeiture, disqualification, and/or a fine in lieu of dismissal.

notes: Not to be confused with the earlier OCA v. Judge Dumayas, A.M. No. RTJ-15-2435, March 6, 2018, where respondent was dismissed from the service; that earlier case is mentioned here only as background. The decision cites "Section 23 of the Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability" without naming the Canon; it is cited the same way here. The decision gives the date of the writ of execution implemented in 2008 as both January 10 and January 16, 2008, so that date is left out of the facts. Marquez, J., took no part; Singh, J., was on leave.
